summary.heading: What is the Doppler effect?
summary.html:
The Doppler effect is the change in the observed frequency (and wavelength) of a wave when the source and observer move relative to each other.
  • Getting closer: higher observed frequency, shorter wavelength. Moving apart: lower frequency, longer wavelength.
  • The source's own frequency doesn't change; only what the observer receives.
  • Only motion along the line joining source and observer matters.
  • It happens for all waves. Sound travels through a medium, so it matters whether the source or the observer moves through the air; for light only the relative motion matters.

summary.heading: Wavefront diagrams: moving source and moving observer
summary.html:
• Moving source: each wavefront is emitted from a new position, so the wavefronts are bunched up in front (shorter wavelength, higher frequency) and spread out behind (longer wavelength, lower frequency).
  • The wave speed doesn't change: it is set by the medium.
  • As a source passes at steady speed, the pitch heard is constant and high, then drops quickly as it passes to a constant low pitch.
  • Moving observer: the wavefronts are evenly spaced (wavelength in the air unchanged), but an observer moving towards the source meets them more often (higher frequency); moving away, less often (lower frequency).

summary.heading: The Doppler effect for light
summary.html:
$$\frac{\Delta f}{f} = \frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} \approx \frac{v}{c}$$
  • Valid when the relative speed $v \ll c$. $\Delta f$ and $\Delta\lambda$ are the shifts; $f$ and $\lambda$ are the emitted values; $v$ is the relative speed along the line of sight.
  • Use the sizes of the shifts and decide the direction from the situation.
  • Moving apart: wavelength increases, redshift. Moving together: blueshift.
  • The speed of light is always $c$; the frequency and wavelength shift.
  • Everyday speeds give tiny shifts (a car: about one part in $10^{7}$), so we never see colours change in traffic.

summary.heading: Uses in astronomy and on Earth
summary.html:
• Each element has its own spectral lines. Comparing a star's lines with laboratory values shows its motion along the line of sight.
  • Expanding universe: almost all distant galaxies are redshifted, more so the further away they are.
  • Rotation: one edge of a spinning star or galaxy is blueshifted and the other redshifted; the difference gives the rotation speed.
  • Binary stars and exoplanets: lines shift back and forth periodically as the star moves towards and away from us.
  • Reflected waves: Doppler ultrasound (blood flow), radar speed guns, weather radar, air traffic control. The shift is roughly twice that for a single trip, because the moving reflector first receives and then re-emits a shifted wave.

summary.heading: Equations for sound: moving source and moving observer
summary.html:
$$f' = f\,\frac{v}{v \pm u_s} \qquad f' = f\,\frac{v \pm u_o}{v}$$
  • $v$ = wave speed in the medium; $u_s$ = source speed; $u_o$ = observer speed.
  • Moving source: the wavelength in the air becomes $(v \mp u_s)T$. Use $-$ when it approaches, $+$ when it recedes.
  • Moving observer: the waves pass at relative speed $v \pm u_o$. Use $+$ when approaching, $-$ when moving away.
  • Choose the sign by reasoning: getting closer must raise $f'$, moving apart must lower it.
  • Problems can ask for the speed of the source or observer (rearrange). Exam problems won't have both moving at once.
  • At the same speed, the two equations give slightly different answers, because sound travels at a fixed speed relative to the air (approaching, a moving source gives the higher frequency). For speeds much less than $v$, both reduce to $\frac{\Delta f}{f} \approx \frac{u}{v}$, the same form as the light equation.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Saying the source's frequency changes.
  • Saying the wave speed changes.
  • Thinking the pitch keeps rising as a source approaches at steady speed.
  • Mixing up redshift (moving apart) and blueshift (moving together).
  • Using $\frac{\Delta f}{f} \approx \frac{v}{c}$ for sound.
  • HL Using the wrong equation: $u_s$ goes in the denominator, $u_o$ in the numerator.
  • HL Choosing the sign by habit instead of checking whether $f'$ should rise or fall.

Hypotheses: Doppler's hypothesis was correct but his example (coloured double stars) was wrong. What should a scientist do when the effect is real but the evidence offered is not?
What would a good test of Doppler's hypothesis have needed in 1842?
Experiments: List the variables in Buys Ballot's train experiment. Which were hard to control, and how could they be improved?
Musicians with good pitch acted as the measuring instruments. What are the strengths and weaknesses of using people as detectors?
Evidence: Redshift alone tells us galaxies move away from us. What extra measurement turned this into evidence for an expanding universe?
Could anything other than motion cause a redshift? How would astronomers rule it out?
Global impact: Doppler ultrasound shows blood flow without surgery. Ask students to compare its risks and benefits with X-ray imaging.
Weather radar gives warnings of severe storms. Who should have access to that data, and should it be free?

oracy.html:
ABC discussion (threes, 8 minutes): each student in turn agrees with, builds on or challenges the last point. Claim: "The siren of an ambulance coming towards you sounds higher because its sound waves travel towards you faster."

  • I agree with … because …
  • Building on that, …
  • I'd challenge that, because …

Listen for: the speed of sound depends on the air, not the source; the moving source catches up a little on each wavefront it has sent out, so the wavelength in front of it is shorter and the observed frequency is higher.

How far can we trust our senses?: Students can hear a passing siren's pitch drop, but they rely on spectrometers for redshift. Is one kind of knowledge more certain?
Our ears can be fooled too. Is direct experience always more trustworthy than an instrument?
Can a theory be right for the wrong reas: Should Doppler get full credit for the effect, given that his main example failed?
Can students think of other ideas accepted for reasons that later turned out to be mistaken?
What does \"moving\" mean?: For sound, the air gives a natural reference frame. For light there is none. What does it mean to say something is "really" moving?
Link to A.5: how did this question lead to special relativity?
How do we know what we can't visit?: List the assumptions astronomers make when they compare a galaxy's spectral lines with a laboratory's. Which would be hardest to check?
How confident should we be in a conclusion that rests on many indirect steps?
